blocks.prompt: The Fruit That Grows Bigger Than You
blocks.text: A pumpkin does not grow on a tree. It grows on a vine that crawls along the ground. The vine can be longer than your whole yard. First the plant makes yellow flowers. The flowers open early in the morning. A bee climbs inside and gets covered in yellow dust. The bee carries that dust to the next flower. That is the job the pumpkin needs done. After the bee visits, a tiny green ball starts to swell at the bottom of the flower. That ball is the baby pumpkin. It drinks water through the vine all summer. It grows heavy. It turns orange. Cut it open and you find the reason it grew at all. Seeds. Hundreds of them.

blocks.prompt: The Fruit Everyone Calls a Vegetable
blocks.text: Ask most people if a pumpkin is a fruit or a vegetable and they will say vegetable. They are wrong, and here is why. A fruit is the part of a plant that holds the seeds. That is the whole rule. Apples hold seeds, so apples are fruit. Pumpkins hold seeds, so pumpkins are fruit too. So are cucumbers, tomatoes, and peppers. The pumpkin plant does not care what we call it. Its only goal is to build a good box for its seeds. First it sends out a vine that crawls across the dirt. The vine grows leaves as big as dinner plates. Then it makes flowers, and here is the tricky part. The flowers open at sunrise and close by lunchtime. They never open again. If a bee does not visit in those few hours, no pumpkin grows. When a bee does visit, the base of the flower begins to swell. All summer that swelling ball drinks water through the vine and fills with sugar and orange color. The skin hardens into a shell. Inside, hundreds of seeds sit in the dark, packed and safe. The pumpkin was never food for us. We just decided it was.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Squash was domesticated in Mexico about 10,000 years ago
One of the oldest crops in the Americas
The Three Sisters: corn, beans, and squash
Squash bees pollinate almost nothing else
Orange comes from beta carotene

blocks.prompt: The Oldest Crop in the Garden
blocks.text: Ten thousand years ago, somewhere in what is now Mexico, people started saving seeds from the best squash plants. Those seeds became the pumpkin. It is one of the oldest crops on Earth, older than corn, older than beans, older than writing. Farmers across the Americas eventually planted all three together in one mound: corn, beans, and squash. The corn shot up and became a pole. The beans climbed the pole and pulled a nutrient called nitrogen out of the air and into the soil, feeding everything around them. The squash sprawled across the ground below, its wide leaves shading out weeds and holding moisture in the dirt, its prickly stems discouraging animals that came to nibble. Three plants, one mound, each doing a job the others could not. Many nations called them the Three Sisters. The pumpkin brought its own helper too. A small brown insect called the squash bee has fed on squash flowers for so long that it now lives almost nowhere else. It wakes before dawn, works the flowers while they are open, and sleeps inside them once they close. Honeybees show up later, after the best hours are gone. And the color? That deep orange comes from a pigment called beta carotene, the same one that makes carrots orange. Your body takes beta carotene apart and rebuilds it into vitamin A, which your eyes use to see in dim light. The pumpkin did not make that pigment for you. It made it for itself. We simply learned that eating it was worth the trouble of growing it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Giant pumpkins are all one variety: Atlantic Giant
World record is above 2,700 pounds
At peak they gain 40 to 50 pounds a day
A giant is roughly 90 percent water
One vine can cover 1,000 square feet
In 1900 the record was about 400 pounds

blocks.prompt: The Weight of a Pumpkin
blocks.text: In October, in a handful of towns across North America and Europe, grown adults gather to watch a fruit be lifted by a crane. The pumpkins arriving on flatbed trailers are not really pumpkins in the ordinary sense. They are pale, lumpy, splitting under their own weight, and they can be heavier than a small car. The current world record sits above 2,700 pounds. A century ago, a 400 pound pumpkin was a marvel. Nothing magic happened. Growers happened. Every giant on the scale descends from a single variety, the Atlantic Giant, bred over decades from unusually large squash by growers who did one simple thing relentlessly: they saved seeds from the biggest fruit and planted them the next year. Do that for fifty seasons and you are steering evolution by hand. The plant itself does the rest, and what it does is startling. A competition pumpkin is allowed exactly one fruit. Every other flower is cut off, so the entire vine, sometimes a thousand square feet of leaves, pours everything it captures into one target. At peak growth, in the hot weeks of midsummer, such a pumpkin can put on forty or fifty pounds in a single day. You cannot see it happening, but you can measure it happening overnight. The vine is drinking hundreds of gallons of water and converting sunlight into sugar, and all of it is arriving in one place. That is also why giants are pale and misshapen. The skin cannot manufacture new cells fast enough to keep up with what is swelling inside it, so it stretches, thins, and sometimes tears. A grower's worst morning is finding a split. And the fruit is not dense, delicious flesh. It is mostly water, roughly ninety percent, wrapped in a shell that is losing the argument. Ask a grower why and the answers turn strange. They talk about soil tests, about wind fences, about waking at three in the morning to check a thermometer. Almost none of them talk about winning. They talk about the fact that a seed the size of your thumbnail, given water, sunlight, and one very patient person, will build something the size of a bathtub in a single summer. The pumpkin is not the point. The proof is.

6.subtitle: A reading and analysis sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Fruit That Grows Bigger Than You

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Botanically a pepo: a berry with a hard rind
Domesticated in southern Mexico about 10,000 years ago
Carving pumpkins and canned pumpkin are different species
The Howden was bred in Massachusetts in the 1970s
Jack-o'-lanterns started as carved turnips in Ireland
Most canned pumpkin is Dickinson squash from Illinois

blocks.prompt: How a Seed Box Became a Face
blocks.text: A pumpkin is not a vegetable. Botanists file it as a pepo: a berry with a hardened rind. Strip away everything familiar about it and what remains is a container. The vine grows the flesh so animals will carry the seeds somewhere useful. The rind hardens so nothing eats them too early. The sugar accumulates as a bribe. Every part of a pumpkin is a solution to the problem of being a plant that cannot move. Humans found that container about ten thousand years ago in the valleys of what is now southern Mexico, and they may have been after the seeds, not the flesh. Wild squash is bitter enough to be close to inedible. But the seeds are oily and full of protein, and the dried rind makes a perfectly good bowl. Generation by generation, growers selected the sweeter mutants and the bigger fruits, and squash became one of the first domesticated plants anywhere in the Americas, older than maize, older than beans, older than any writing on Earth. Later, across the continent, farmers planted it in mounds beside corn and beans, where its enormous leaves shaded out weeds and held moisture in the soil. The corn was the pole, the beans fed the ground, and the squash defended the floor. Three plants, one mound, no wasted space. The carved face arrived from somewhere else entirely. In Ireland and Scotland, people marking Samhain carved lanterns from turnips and beets, cutting crude faces into them and setting a coal inside. The name they used, jack-o'-lantern, had earlier belonged to the strange lights that hover over bogs at night, the kind that lure travelers off the path. When Irish families emigrated to America in the nineteenth century, they met a fruit that was enormous, hollow, soft-walled, and everywhere. The turnip never stood a chance. What happened next is the part worth thinking about. The pumpkin on your porch is almost certainly a Howden, a variety bred in Massachusetts in the 1970s for one purpose: to be carved. It is tall, evenly ribbed, deep orange, thin-walled, and largely tasteless. Meanwhile the pumpkin in the can in your pantry is usually not orange at all. It is a tan, oblong Dickinson squash, grown mostly in a few counties of Illinois, and it never sees a porch. The two are not even the same species. We split the pumpkin into two separate crops: one bred for flavor, one bred for faces. The face industry is enormous. Americans grow well over a billion pounds of pumpkins a year, and a large share of that tonnage is set outdoors, admired for a week, and then thrown away. Buried in a landfill, that flesh rots without oxygen and releases methane, a greenhouse gas considerably more potent than carbon dioxide. A fruit engineered by evolution to feed animals, and then reengineered by us for ten thousand years, now frequently ends its life as a source of emissions. None of which is an argument against carving one. It is an argument for noticing what you are holding. That pumpkin is a bribe, an heirloom, a migration story, and a designed product, all at once. It carries seeds that would grow if you let them. Most of us scrape them out, throw them in the trash, and cut a face into the box.
